Spanish 1 — Teacher Manual

Optima Academy Online · Course code 0708340

Your Canvas courseSemester 1: ____________ · Semester 2: ____________
Shape9 modules per semester · 10 lessons per module · about 40 minutes a day
Where students landNovice Mid → Novice High
Comes after / beforeNo prerequisite → Spanish 1 → Spanish 2

1. Start here

Spanish 1 is a full-year, entry-level course. Students arrive with no Spanish. They leave able to introduce themselves, describe people and daily life, talk about food and free time, and narrate simple events in the past.

The course is pan-Hispanic and Latin-American-first. Each module features a different country rather than treating Spain as the default, and usted is taught as the normal respectful form across Latin America rather than as something stiff or old-fashioned. Vosotros is introduced as European and clearly labelled.

The course teaches itself. Every explanation, model sentence, audio clip and practice activity a student needs is already on the lesson pages. You are not preparing or delivering content.

Your job is three things:

  1. Grade the Tarea oral — one per student per module — and, in Semester 1 only, the VR project once in the semester. These are the only items that need a human. Everything else grades itself.
  2. Notice who is stuck and reach out early. Section 6 shows you where to look.
  3. Answer questions about Spanish, about the countries featured, and about what a task is asking.

Budget roughly 20–30 minutes of grading per student per semester, concentrated in the Tareas orales. Section 3 breaks it down.

2. Before term starts — about fifteen minutes

Do these once. None of them announce themselves if they are wrong; the course simply behaves incorrectly all semester.

Turn on weighted grading — do this first

Course → Assignments → ⋮ (top right) → Assignment Groups Weight → tick "Weight final grade based on assignment groups."

It is not in Settings, which is where most people look. Until that box is ticked, Canvas ignores the percentages and grades on raw points instead — which would badly distort this course, since the nine Vocabulary Checks are worth 225 raw points and the Final only 48. The percentage fields only unlock after you tick the box.

Then confirm the weights match Section 7.

Confirm students can complete the work

Every lesson page should be set to Mark as Done, and every quiz and assignment to Submit the Assignment. Each lesson page ends with a banner telling students to click Mark as Done — if that requirement is missing, you are telling them to press a button that is not there, and nothing tracks their progress.

Confirm nothing is gated

On Demand courses do not throttle progress. There should be no module prerequisites, no minimum-score requirements, and no "students must move through requirements in sequential order." Students may work ahead at their own pace.

Standing settings

  • Vocabulary Check: 1 attempt, 15-minute limit. This is deliberate — see Section 4.
  • Grammar Quiz: 2 attempts, no time limit.
  • Lengua en acción: 1 attempt, no time limit.
  • Final exam: 1 attempt, 75-minute limit.

3. Your week

Modules run two weeks. In a normal week you have one round of Tareas orales arriving from roughly half your students.

TaskWhenAbout how long
Tarea oral — listen and score against a 3-line rubricOne per student per module3–5 min per student
VR project — read, watch, score against a 5-line rubricSemester 1 only, once20–25 min per student
Checking who has fallen behindWeekly15 min
Answering questionsOngoingVaries

Everything else — Vocabulary Checks, Grammar Quizzes, Lengua en acción, the Mapa, both Finals — is auto-graded and needs nothing from you unless a student disputes a score.

The VR project is the one week that bites — in Semester 1. It lands at the end of that semester alongside the Final. Start grading them as they arrive rather than waiting for the deadline.

4. What you grade

Each module is worth 90 points:

ItemPointsGraded byNotes
Vocabulary Check25CanvasListening-based. 1 attempt, 15 min.
Grammar Quiz30Canvas2 attempts. Includes listening items.
Lengua en acción20CanvasWritten production, auto-scored. 1 attempt.
Tarea oral15You — rubricStudents record in the browser.

Plus, once per semester: the Final exam (48 pts in S1, 50 in S2). Semester 1 also has the VR project (100 pts); Semester 2 has no semester project. Semester 1 also has a Mapa del Mundo Hispano quiz (8 pts, 2 attempts) in the final module; it sits in an Extra Credit group weighted at 0%, so it cannot move a grade — treat it as a challenge, not a requirement, and say so if students ask.

Two separate queues. Quizzes and assignments land in different places in Canvas. This course is fully auto-graded on the quiz side, but the Tareas orales and the S1 VR project are assignments and will sit in SpeedGrader waiting for you. Check both.

Why the Vocabulary Check is one attempt and timed. It is built ear-first: most items play audio and give no written Spanish to read from. One attempt with a clock keeps it a listening measure rather than a look-it-up exercise. Students who ask for a retake are usually asking to turn it into a different assessment — the Grammar Quiz, with its two attempts, is where the second chance lives.

5. Grading the rubric items

Tarea oral — 15 points, every module

Students record a short spoken response in the browser. Same three criteria every module, all year.

CriterionPointsWhat earns full marks
Task Completion5Answers the prompt fully, at the length asked for
Language Accuracy5Uses the module's structures correctly enough to be understood
Pronunciation & Fluency5Comprehensible to a sympathetic Spanish speaker; runs without long stalls

Grade for communication, not for an accent. At Novice level the question is whether a patient Spanish speaker would understand them. Hesitation, an audibly-reading-from-notes delivery, and an English-flavoured accent are all normal and should not cost points. Reserve deductions for what actually blocks meaning: a verb form that changes who is doing the action, ser where estar is required in a way that reverses the sense, or a response that answers a different question.

A weak trilled rr is not worth a deduction at this level. Very few first-year students produce one, and the course does not ask them to.

Students are told to write and rehearse their script first. That is deliberate and not cheating.

VR project — 100 points, Semester 1 only

Semester 1: Mi puesto en el mercado. Students build a scene, narrate it in Spanish, and write a reflection. Solo work producing one artifact — not a live role-play.

Semester 2 has no semester project. Mi diario de viaje was withdrawn on 2026-09-21 and its 10% moved into the Grammar Quizzes and Vocabulary Checks. Nothing to grade here in S2.

Semester 1

CriterionPoints
Preparación / Preparation20
Composición / VR composition25
Precisión del idioma / Language accuracy25
Narración hablada / Spoken narration20
Reflexión / Reflection10

The two heaviest criteria are language and composition. A beautiful stall with no Spanish is a low score; a plain stall described well in Spanish is a high one. Say that to students before they start.

6. Spotting a student who is stuck

What you can and cannot see

You can see: which lessons a student has marked done, every quiz and assignment score, per-question breakdowns on quizzes, and everything students write in the module check-in surveys.

You cannot see anything students do in the practice activities inside the lesson pages. Those give instant feedback on the page and record nothing, anywhere — not to Canvas, not even to the student's own browser. There is no report and no setting that changes this. Do not go looking for it.

So for the first six days of a module you have pace, not comprehension. The first real signal is the Vocabulary Check on day 7. A student can look perfectly on track and still be lost. The check-in surveys are what bridge that gap — they are your only early comprehension signal.

Where to look

To answerGo to
Who is behind?Modules → View Progress
Who is struggling, and with what?Gradebook, then the quiz's Statistics for a per-question breakdown
What did students say they found hard?Quizzes → the module check-in → Survey Statistics, or Student Analysis for individual written answers
The check-in surveys are ungraded, so they have no gradebook column and will not open in SpeedGrader. Read them through Survey Statistics or the Student Analysis download.

A weekly routine — 15 minutes

  1. Modules → View Progress: note anyone more than three days behind.
  2. Gradebook: scan the week's Vocabulary Checks and Grammar Quizzes for anyone under 70%.
  3. Check-in surveys: skim the written answers for confusion worth a reply.
  4. Send three to five short personal messages. Early and brief beats late and thorough.

7. The course at a glance

Each module: 90 points — Vocabulary Check 25 · Grammar Quiz 30 · Lengua en acción 20 · Tarea oral 15

Final grade weighting:

Semester 2 has no project; its 10% sits in the two auto-graded categories.

Two thirds of the grade sits in auto-graded work students can prepare for directly. The Tarea oral is weighted at 15% — enough that students take it seriously, low enough that one nervous recording does not sink a grade.

8. Module reference

Each module features a country and a short virtue portrait of a figure from the Spanish-speaking world.

Semester 1

ModuleThemeLanguage focusVirtue portrait
M0El mundo hispanoSounds and vowels, greetings, courtesy, numbers—
M1Quién soyIdentity, nationalities; serCourage · Simón Bolívar
M2La escuelaSchool; -ar verbsService · Roberto Clemente
M3Ser vs. EstarFeelings and places; the contrastPerseverance · Frida Kahlo
M4La familiaFamily; tener and its expressionsResponsibility · Rigoberta Menchú
M5La comidaFood; gustar and object pronounsCourtesy · San Martín de Porres
M6El tiempo libreHobbies; -er / -ir verbsHonesty · Bartolomé de las Casas
M7Cómo eresDescription; adjective agreement and placementSelf-Government · José de San Martín
M8Describir a las personasFull S1 synthesis (capstone)The seven together

M0 replaces the Grammar Quiz with a Pronunciation and Sound Quiz (30 pts, same weight). M8 also carries the VR project and the Mapa del Mundo Hispano.

Two men named San Martín. M5 features San Martín de Porres, the Peruvian friar. M7 features José de San Martín, the Argentine general who liberated Perú. Students conflate them every year. Use the full name each time and the confusion largely disappears.

Semester 2

M2La casaHousehold, stem-changing verbsChile
M3La ciudadThe city, places and directionsMéxico
M4La rutina diariaReflexive verbsEcuador

M9 carries no project — Semester 2 ends with the Final Exam.

9. Common struggles

Ser versus estar (M3). The single hardest thing in first-year Spanish, and the course teaches the two verbs together rather than weeks apart — deliberately, so students build the contrast rather than defaulting to ser for everything. Expect it to stay wobbly for months. The usable rule is permanent-versus-current, but the honest answer is that it takes repetition. Do not re-explain the rule to a struggling student; send them back to M3's practice, where the contrast is drilled in pairs.

Gustar works backwards (M5). Me gusta la pizza is not "I like pizza" structurally — it is closer to "pizza is pleasing to me," so the thing liked is the subject and the person is an object pronoun. Students who learn it as a fixed phrase do fine; students who try to translate word-for-word stall. The fix is to treat me gusta / te gusta / le gusta as vocabulary first and analyse it later.

Gender and adjective agreement (M7 especially). Students meet gender in M0 and then have to make adjectives agree in number and gender all at once in M7, which is deliberately the most intensive module in the semester. If a student is drowning there, the problem is usually gender from earlier, not the adjectives themselves.

The five vowels. Spanish vowels are pure and unchanging; English speakers glide them. This is the first thing M0 teaches, and it pays off all year — a student with clean vowels is understood even when the grammar wobbles. Point students back to the M0 audio rather than describing the sounds.

The rolled rr. M0 Lesson 0.03 teaches the pero / perro contrast with native-speaker recordings. Most first-year students cannot produce a trill, and the course does not require one. Reassure them — being understood does not depend on it.

The preterite (S2 M6–M7). The past tense arrives late and is deliberately split: regular forms in M6, high-frequency irregulars in M7. Students who struggle in M7 usually have not consolidated M6. Resist letting them push on — the irregulars only make sense against a solid regular pattern.

10. Platforms and questions

  • VR project (ARTHUR) — Semester 1 only. Students work solo and submit one artifact — a scene plus spoken

narration and a written reflection. There is no live session to schedule and no partner to coordinate. Semester 2 has no project.

  • Audio. Every vocabulary word, model sentence and reading has a recorded clip on the lesson page.

Students should be listening daily, not only for the Vocabulary Check.

  • Speaking recordings. Students record directly in Canvas; no external app or account is needed.

If a recording fails to upload, the usual cause is a browser blocking microphone access.

Questions about the course build, or a setting that looks wrong: David Waters — dwaters@optimaed.com

pages.title: Final Exam — Part D grading guide
pages.html:
For teachers only. The Semester 2 Final Exam is auto-graded except Part D, four short writing prompts worth 2 points each. Grade them in SpeedGrader against the target answers and the scoring guide below.

Part D · Expresión escrita 8 pts

Four prompts · 2 pts each · hand-graded. Budget ~3 minutes per student.

Paste the prompt column verbatim. Each prompt gives the student the exact sentence to write, in English, and names the structure and the módulo it comes from. Two reasons this shape was chosen over an open prompt: the student cannot be unsure what is wanted, and there is a single target answer to grade against, so two teachers reach the same mark. ⚠ Do not print the target answer or the notes column to students. The accent strip from Part C sits in the quiz instructions and stays visible here.
Prompt — shown to the student exactly as writtenTarget answer (builder/grader only)Grading notesModPts
1. Write in Spanish: “Yesterday, I ate pizza with my family.”
This sentence needs the preterite — the past tense from Módulos 6 and 7.		Ayer comí pizza con mi familia.Preterite comí required. Accept comi (no accent), word order Comí pizza con mi familia ayer, and mi familia y yo comimos.M62
2. Write in Spanish: “I get up at seven o’clock.”
This sentence needs a reflexive verb in the present — from Módulo 4.		Me levanto a las siete.The pronoun me must be there and must precede the verb. Accept Yo me levanto a las siete. Levanto a las siete (no pronoun) scores 1.M42
3. Write in Spanish: “I am going to visit the museum.”
This sentence needs ir + a + infinitive — the near future from Módulo 1.		Voy a visitar el museo.All three parts required: voy + a + infinitive. Voy visitar (missing a) scores 1. Visito el museo (present, not near future) scores 0.M12
4. Write in Spanish: “The summer is better than the winter.”
This sentence needs a comparative — from Módulo 8.		El verano es mejor que el invierno.mejor que required. Accept más bueno que is not accepted — mejor is the form taught. Missing que scores 1.M82

Scoring — apply per prompt

PtsWhat it looks like
2The sentence matches the target in meaning and the named structure is formed correctly. Minor spelling or accent slips do not cost the point — comi for comí is still 2.
1The named structure is attempted but mis-formed (wrong ending, missing reflexive pronoun, ir without a), or the meaning is only partly recoverable.
0The named structure is absent, the sentence is in English, or nothing is written.
teacher note. Score the structure, not the ambition. A short correct sentence earns 2; a long adventurous one with the wrong tense earns 1. Say so to students beforehand — it stops them over-reaching and losing marks they had already earned.

assignments.title: Module 1 — Tarea oral
assignments.html:
Record yourself describing this week's weather and your plans. Include one sentence about the weather (Hoy hace…) and at least two plans using ir a + a verb (Voy a… / Vamos a…). Speak in complete sentences. ~20–40 seconds.

Example: Esta semana hace sol. Hoy voy a estudiar español. Mañana mi familia y yo vamos a ir a la playa.

Use Canvas’s Record/Upload Media button to record your answer. You may re-record before you submit.

assignments.title: Module 2 — Tarea oral
assignments.html:
Record yourself describing your home and the chores you do. Name at least two rooms of your home, and use at least two stem-changing verbs (for example querer, poder, preferir, jugar) to say what you and your family want, can, or prefer to do. Speak in complete sentences. ~30–45 seconds.

Example: En mi casa hay una cocina y dos dormitorios. Yo quiero ordenar mi habitación. Los sábados nosotros limpiamos juntos.

Use Canvas’s Record/Upload Media button to record your answer. You may re-record before you submit.

assignments.title: Module 3 — Tarea oral
assignments.html:
Record yourself doing two things: (1) give directions to a real place in your town, using words like derecho, a la derecha / izquierda, la esquina, el semáforo, and cuadras; and (2) say what you do downtown in at least two sentences using irregular-yo verbs (salgo, hago, veo, doy, pongo…). Speak in complete sentences. ~30–45 seconds.

Example: «Para llegar al mercado, sigues derecho dos cuadras y doblas a la derecha en el semáforo. En el centro, yo salgo temprano, veo los museos y doy un paseo por la plaza.»

Use Canvas’s Record/Upload Media button to record your answer. You may re-record before you submit.

assignments.title: Module 4 — Tarea oral
assignments.html:
Record yourself narrating your morning routine in order. Give at least four steps, each a reflexive verb (me despierto, me levanto, me ducho, me visto…), and connect them with sequence words (primero, después, luego, por último). Speak in the yo form. ~30–45 seconds.

Example: Primero me despierto a las seis. Después me levanto y me ducho. Luego me visto. Y por último desayuno.

Use Canvas’s Record/Upload Media button to record your answer. You may re-record before you submit.

assignments.title: Module 5 — Tarea oral
assignments.html:
Record yourself speaking Spanish for about 30–45 seconds. Choose ONE: (A) role-play ordering a meal at a restaurant (greet the camarero, ask for the menú, order a food, ask for la cuenta), or (B) talk about a food you know how to make (say what it is, that you sabes cocinarlo, and where you buy the ingredients). Whichever you choose, include at least one saber/conocer and one direct-object pronoun (lo/la/los/las).

Example: Sé preparar una tortilla española. Necesito huevos; los compro en el supermercado. Conozco un buen mercado.

Use Canvas’s Record/Upload Media button to record your answer. You may re-record before you submit.

assignments.title: Module 6 — Tarea oral
assignments.html:
Record yourself saying three true sentences about what you did last weekend (el fin de semana pasado). Use the regular preterite, a different verb each time, and start each sentence with a time word. Speak in complete sentences. ~30–45 seconds.

Example: El fin de semana pasado caminé en el parque. El sábado preparé la cena. El domingo nadé.

Use Canvas’s Record/Upload Media button to record your answer. You may re-record before you submit.

assignments.title: Module 7 — Tarea oral
assignments.html:
Record yourself telling about a trip you took (real or imagined). Say three true things in the past using the irregular preterite: where you went (fui / fuimos a…), one thing you did (hice…), and where you were / stayed or what it was like (estuve… / fue…). Use at least three M7 travel words. Speak in complete sentences. ~30–45 seconds.

Example: El año pasado fui a Perú. Hice una excursión a Machu Picchu con un guía. El viaje fue una gran aventura.

Use Canvas’s Record/Upload Media button to record your answer. You may re-record before you submit.

assignments.title: Module 8 — Tarea oral
assignments.html:
Describe a celebration. Record yourself giving three true sentences: (1) say what someone is doing right now using the present progressive (está / están + -ando/-iendo), (2) name one thing you see or hear at the fiesta using this module's vocabulary, and (3) make one comparison using más…que, menos…que, mejor, peor, or tan…como. Speak in complete sentences. ~30–45 seconds.

Example: El cantante está cantando una canción. Hay fuegos artificiales en el festival. La cumbia es más alegre que la balada.

Use Canvas’s Record/Upload Media button to record your answer. You may re-record before you submit.

assignments.title: Module 9 — Tarea oral
assignments.html:
Record a self-narrative in Spanish, about 45–60 seconds. Tell the story of an experience in three parts: (1) a past experience — something you did, using the preterite (e.g. a trip, a weekend, a celebration); (2) a description — say what the place or the experience was/is like (ser/estar + adjective); and (3) a future plan — what you are going to do next, using ir a + infinitive. Speak in complete sentences and connect your ideas.” Provide the worked model in the lesson — Sofía's story from Lesson 9.04 (passage/s2m9-experiencia.mp3) is the template: a description, a past trip in the preterite, and a plan with voy a.
